chief_complaint: difficulty falling asleep taking over 2 hours every night with daytime fatigue and anxiety about sleep performance
hpi_details: She has had 6 months of difficulty initiating sleep, often lying awake for more than 2 hours while clock-watching, with daytime fatigue. She has not yet started treatment and is suitable for CBT-I after assessment of other sleep, medical, psychiatric, and substance-related contributors.
ideas: She thinks anxiety about sleep is perpetuating the insomnia.
concerns: She is worried that fatigue is impairing her daytime function.
expectations: She hopes to receive structured sleep retraining techniques and a short-term prescription sleep aid to break her cycle of sleepless nights.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Chronic insomnia disorder: evaluation and management
core_concepts: Chronic insomnia disorder is difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep despite adequate opportunity, with daytime impairment for at least 3 months.
Use a sleep diary and assess sleep schedule, sleep opportunity, depression, anxiety, mania, substance use, medicines, sleep apnoea, restless legs syndrome, and circadian disorders.
CBT-I is first-line and includes stimulus control, sleep scheduling, cognitive work, and relapse prevention.
Medication is not a substitute for CBT-I; if used, it requires individualized risk review, short duration, and monitoring for sedation, dependence, falls, and interactions.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: difficulty falling asleep taking over 2 hours every night with daytime fatigue and anxiety about sleep performance

Key HPI features: 46F presenting with 6 months of severe conditioned insomnia spending hours lying awake in bed worrying about clock-watching responding to first-line Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I: stimulus control and sleep restriction protocols).
Objective/Exam findings: Mental-state examination, medication and substance review, and targeted examination or testing guided by suspected sleep or medical disorder.
common_misconceptions: Treating chronic insomnia with sleep-hygiene advice alone.
Overlooking bipolar-spectrum symptoms, depression, substance use, sleep apnoea, or restless legs syndrome.
Assuming a sedative is harmless or effective long term.
dangerous_errors: Missing suicidality, mania, psychosis, severe depression, or intoxication/withdrawal.
Starting sedative-hypnotics without checking alcohol or opioid use, falls risk, driving risk, interactions, or dependence history.
management_principles: Offer CBT-I and a sleep diary; advise against clock-watching and prolonged wakefulness in bed.
Address contributory psychiatric, medical, medication, and substance factors.
Use medication only after shared decision-making and appropriate safety review, with planned follow-up.
Urgently assess suicidal intent, mania, psychosis, severe functional deterioration, or dangerous impairment such as drowsy driving.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: She reports 6 months of sleep-onset insomnia, clock-watching, and daytime fatigue despite opportunity to sleep.
reference_soap.objective: Review sleep diary, sleep opportunity and schedule, mental state, substances and medications; screen for apnoea, restless legs, circadian disorder, depression, anxiety, and mania as indicated.
reference_soap.assessment: Chronic insomnia disorder is likely, subject to assessment of comorbid sleep, psychiatric, medical, and substance-related causes.
reference_soap.plan: Offer CBT-I and follow progress with a sleep diary. Treat contributing conditions. Consider short-term medication only with individualized safety assessment and follow-up. Urgently evaluate suicidal intent, mania, psychosis, or unsafe impairment.

teaching.one_liner: Psychiatric evaluation for patient presenting with difficulty falling asleep taking over 2 hours every night with daytime fatigue and anxiety about sleep performance.

must_ask.say: How long does it take you to fall asleep, and do you wake up during the night?
Do you find yourself watching the clock or worrying about not being able to sleep?
What do you do while lying in bed besides trying to sleep — reading, phone use, or lying awake?
How does the poor sleep affect your mood or functioning during the day?
Do you snore, have leg movements at night, or use caffeine or alcohol close to bedtime?

history.answer: I have been having a really hard time falling asleep for the past six months, and the daytime fatigue is exhausting me.
My main struggle is falling asleep in the first place; once I finally drift off, I generally stay asleep through the night.
This has been happening almost every night, about five or six nights a week, for the past six months.
It started six months ago during a tight project deadline at work, but the sleep problem stayed even after the project finished.
I get into bed at ten thirty in the evening, but I toss and turn for over two hours before falling asleep, and I get up at six thirty every morning.
I feel tense and anxious as soon as my head hits the pillow because I worry whether I will be able to fall asleep and how exhausted I will be tomorrow.
I keep checking the alarm clock on my nightstand every few minutes, and sometimes I look at my phone in bed when I cannot fall asleep.
I feel drained and sluggish throughout the day, and it takes more effort to concentrate at work, though I have never dozed off while driving.
I avoid taking naps during the day because I am worried it will make falling asleep at night even harder.
I drink one cup of black coffee in the morning around eight, but I avoid caffeine in the afternoon and evening.
I never drink alcohol to help me fall asleep, and I only have a glass of wine on occasional weekends.
My husband tells me I do not snore loudly, and he has never noticed me stop breathing or choking during the night.
No, I do not wake up with morning headaches or a parched mouth.
No, I have never felt an unpleasant urge to move my legs or creeping sensations in them at bedtime.
No, I work steady daytime office hours from nine to five and have never done shift work.
I do not feel depressed and I still enjoy spending time with my family; my mood is just weighed down by feeling tired.
I do not have generalized worries about everyday matters like money or health; my anxiety is strictly about falling asleep.
No, I have never had thoughts of harming myself or wishing I were dead.
No, I have never had periods where I felt energized or abnormally high after only a couple hours of sleep; I desperately want to sleep.
No, I do not have chronic joint pain, heartburn, palpitations, or night sweats keeping me awake.
No, once I fall asleep, I rarely have to get up to use the restroom during the night.
Our bedroom is dark, quiet, and kept at a cool temperature, and my husband is a quiet sleeper.
I tried over-the-counter melatonin and chamomile tea for a few weeks, but they did not help me fall asleep any faster.
I think my own worry and frustration about not sleeping has turned into a vicious cycle that keeps me awake.
I am worried that this ongoing exhaustion will eventually impair my daytime performance and harm my health.
I hope to leave with a clear plan to reset my sleep routine and maybe a mild sleep aid to help break this cycle while I work on it.
I was diagnosed with high blood pressure and mild high cholesterol about three years ago.
I had an appendectomy about twenty years ago without any complications, but no other surgeries or hospitalizations.
I take lisinopril ten milligrams once every morning for my blood pressure.
No, I do not have any allergies to medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or nicotine products.
I work as an accountant and live in a house with my husband.
My mother has high blood pressure, but no one in my family has a history of sleep disorders or psychiatric conditions.
My periods are regular every twenty-eight days with my last period two weeks ago, and my husband had a vasectomy so there is no possibility of pregnancy.

Alert woman appearing tired with subtle dark circles under her eyes, well-groomed, and in no acute distress.
Oral cavity is clear with normal uvula, non-enlarged tonsils, and a Mallampati class II airway without crowding or macroglossia.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, smooth, non-tender, and moves symmetrically with swallowing without palpable nodules or goiter.
Normal S1 and S2 with regular rate and rhythm, and no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with vesicular breath sounds and no wheezing, rhonchi, or crackles.
Both lower legs are symmetric without swelling, warmth, tenderness, or involuntary movements.
No resting, postural, or kinetic tremors observed in outstretched hands.
Cooperative and oriented to person, place, and time; affect is anxious when discussing bedtime, but thought process is linear, mood is euthymic, and no suicidal ideation or psychosis is present.
